claims.text: A machine-learning framework trained on extensive high-temperature oxidation data can identify processing routes that promote protective oxide-scale formation.
Dense protective oxide scales can significantly improve the oxidation resistance of oxidation-prone alloys.
Failure to form a dense protective oxide scale is associated with high oxidation susceptibility.
Experimental oxidation data can include oxidation kinetics, mass gain, and oxide phase-composition measurements.
The proposed machine-learning approach can integrate oxidation kinetics, activation energies, and oxide compositions to guide processing and composition changes.
The method is intended for prolonged exposure in high-temperature oxidizing environments.
A dense protective oxide layer slows substrate oxidation kinetics.
Cr2O3 or Al2O3 can serve as the dense, adherent protective layer in the proposed alloys.
An ML model can correlate processing parameters, composition variables, and oxidation performance to predict conditions that promote protective oxides.
ML-guided processing or composition changes produce a microstructure favoring slow-growing, adherent oxide scales.
Formation of a protective oxide scale is associated with parabolic oxidation behavior and low mass gain.
Materials processed under ML-guided conditions will have lower oxidation rates and lower thermogravimetric weight gain than conventionally processed baseline materials.
Materials processed under ML-guided conditions will have improved high-temperature performance relative to the baseline.
Conventional trial-and-error processing has historically produced non-optimized oxide layers and higher oxidation rates.
ML effectiveness depends on the quality, range, completeness, accuracy, and representativeness of its training data.
The ML model may have limited predictive capability for alloy systems or processing conditions outside its training data.
Thermogravimetric analysis can measure oxidation-associated mass gain during high-temperature exposure.
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy can characterize oxide-scale phase composition and morphology.
